title: 2 Kings 22:8–20
context: Hilkiah finds the book of the law in the temple. When it is read to Josiah, he tears his clothes and sends officials to inquire of the LORD through the prophetess Huldah, who confirms coming judgment but promises Josiah he will die before it falls. Many identify the book with Deuteronomy or part of it, though the text does not say so.

verses.text: Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the book of the law in the LORD’s house.” Hilkiah delivered the book to Shaphan, and he read it.
verses.arminianNotes: Hilkiah says, “I have found the book of the law in the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers see the rediscovery of God’s word as a turning point for the nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s word recovered at a crucial time. Many interpreters connect this book with Deuteronomy or part of it, though the text does not identify it precisely.

verses.text: Shaphan the scribe came to the king, and brought the king word again, and said, “Your servants have emptied out the money that was found in the house, and have delivered it into the hands of the workmen who have the oversight of the LORD’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes: Shaphan reports that the money has been delivered to the workmen. Arminian readers see the routine report preceding the extraordinary news about the book.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator placing the ordinary before the remarkable. The account shows faithful administration while the significance of the book is still unfolding.

verses.text: Shaphan the scribe told the king, saying, “Hilkiah the priest has delivered a book to me.” Then Shaphan read it before the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Shaphan says, “Hilkiah the priest has delivered a book to me,” and reads it before the king. Arminian readers see God’s word reaching the king through faithful servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word read aloud before the king. The understated introduction of the book contrasts with the profound effect it will have.

verses.text: When the king had heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes.
verses.arminianNotes: When the king hears the words of the book, “he tore his clothes.” Arminian readers see a heart that responds to God’s word with humility and grief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word producing conviction in the king. Readers in both traditions commonly treat this response as a model of receiving God’s word with seriousness.

verses.text: The king commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Achbor the son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The king commands Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah. Arminian readers see Josiah acting immediately on his conviction, involving trusted leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the king responding with urgency. The naming of officials shows that the matter is treated as a concern for the whole nation.

verses.text: “Go inquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found; for great is the LORD’s wrath that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not listened to the words of this book, to do according to all that which is written concerning us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Josiah says, “Go inquire of the LORD for me, and for the people … for great is the LORD’s wrath that is kindled against us.” Arminian readers see the king acknowledging inherited guilt and seeking God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Josiah confessing that “our fathers have not listened to the words of this book.” His response combines personal humility with concern for the whole people.

verses.text: So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe (now she lived in Jerusalem in the second quarter); and they talked with her.
verses.arminianNotes: The officials go to Huldah the prophetess in Jerusalem’s second quarter. Arminian readers see God speaking through a woman prophet whom the king’s officials recognize as authoritative.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Huldah consulted as a true prophet of the LORD. The narrator gives her family details, establishing her identity and credibility.

verses.text: She said to them, “The LORD the God of Israel says, ‘Tell the man who sent you to me,
verses.arminianNotes: She says, “The LORD the God of Israel says, ‘Tell the man who sent you to me.’” Arminian readers see Huldah speaking boldly with divine authority to the king’s representatives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Huldah delivering God’s word without hesitation. Her opening formula marks her message as the LORD’s, not her own opinion.

verses.text: “The LORD says, ‘Behold, I will bring evil on this place and on its inhabitants, even all the words of the book which the king of Judah has read.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I will bring evil on this place and on its inhabitants, even all the words of the book.” Arminian readers see God confirming the warnings written in the book.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God affirming that his word will be fulfilled. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as shared ground on the seriousness of God’s covenant warnings.

verses.text: Because they have forsaken me and have burned incense to other gods, that they might provoke me to anger with all the work of their hands, therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and it will not be quenched.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “Because they have forsaken me and have burned incense to other gods … my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and it will not be quenched.” Arminian readers see judgment grounded in persistent idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s wrath as his just response to idolatry. The phrase “it will not be quenched” anticipates the narrator’s explanation in 23:26–27.

verses.text: But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD, tell him, “The LORD the God of Israel says, ‘Concerning the words which you have heard,
verses.arminianNotes: To the king who inquired, Huldah sends a separate word. Arminian readers see God distinguishing the king’s response from the nation’s rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God addressing Josiah personally. The shift from the people to the king highlights how God regards those who humble themselves.

verses.text: because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before the LORD when you heard what I spoke against this place and against its inhabitants, that they should become a desolation and a curse, and have torn your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you,’ says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “… because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before the LORD … I also have heard you.” Arminian readers see God responding to Josiah’s humble repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God honoring a tender heart, which many in this tradition regard as itself a work of God’s grace. This is shared ground on repentance under the word.

verses.text: ‘Therefore behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the evil which I will bring on this place.’ ” ’ ” So they brought this message back to the king.
verses.arminianNotes: “… you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the evil which I will bring on this place.” Arminian readers see mercy shown to Josiah in sparing him the coming disaster.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s kindness to Josiah. Readers in this tradition commonly understand “in peace” as dying before the catastrophe, given the account of his death in 23:29.
